review:
There is a scene in which a bear teaches a prison canteen to make marmalade, and the prison becomes a nicer place, and the film asks you to accept this without irony. That it succeeds is the whole achievement. Paul King has made a comedy with no cynicism in it at all, which in 2026 reads as something close to an avant-garde gesture.

Hugh Grant, playing a washed-up actor with a costume trunk and a grudge, gives what may be the best performance of his career precisely because he refuses to condescend to the material. He is not slumming. He commits to a dog costume with the same seriousness other actors bring to Lear, and the film is generous enough to give him a curtain call.

The pop-up book sequence — Paddington walking his aunt through a paper London that folds up around them — is the most purely beautiful thing in any recent children's film. It lasts ninety seconds and justifies the entire production.

The thesis is stated plainly and repeated without embarrassment: if you are kind and polite, the world will be right. The film knows this is not true. It argues for it anyway, and it wins.
